paragraphs: “I have to make one confession,” Ivan began. “I never could understand how a person can love his neighbors. It’s exactly the neighbors, to my mind, that one can’t love. One might love people at a distance. I once read somewhere about John the Merciful, a saint. A hungry, frozen beggar came to him, and he took the man into his bed, held him in his arms, and breathed into his mouth, which was putrid and loathsome from some terrible disease. I’m convinced he did that out of ‘self-laceration,’ the self-laceration of falsity, for the sake of a charity imposed by duty, as a penance laid on him. For anyone to love a man, the man must stay hidden. As soon as he shows his face, love is gone.”

“Father Zossima has spoken of that more than once,” Alyosha observed. “He, too, said that a man’s face often keeps people who aren’t practiced in love from loving him. But still, there’s a great deal of love in mankind, almost Christ-like love. I know that myself, Ivan.”

“Well, I know nothing of it so far, and I can’t understand it, and the countless mass of mankind is with me there. The question is whether that’s due to men’s bad qualities or whether it’s part of their nature. As I see it, Christ-like love for men is a miracle that’s impossible on earth. He was God. But we are not gods. Suppose I suffer terribly, for instance. Another person can never know how much I suffer, because he is another and not I. And what’s more, a man is seldom willing to admit that someone else is suffering (as though it were a distinction). Why won’t he admit it, do you think? Because I smell bad, because I have a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. Besides, there is suffering and suffering. Degrading, humiliating suffering that humbles me—hunger, for instance—my benefactor may allow me. But when you come to higher suffering—for an idea, say—he will very rarely admit that. Perhaps my face strikes him as not at all what he imagines a man should have who suffers for an idea. And so he withdraws his favor from me at once, and not at all from badness of heart. Beggars, especially genteel beggars, should never show themselves, but ask for charity through the newspapers. One can love one’s neighbors in the abstract, or even at a distance, but up close it’s almost impossible. If it were like the stage, in the ballet, where beggars come on in silken rags and tattered lace and beg for alms dancing gracefully, then one might enjoy looking at them. But even then we wouldn’t love them. Enough of that, though. I only wanted to show you my point of view. I meant to speak of the suffering of mankind in general, but we had better keep to the sufferings of children. That cuts the scope of my argument down to a tenth of what it would be. Still, we’d better stick to the children, though it weakens my case. But, in the first place, children can be loved even up close, even when they’re dirty, even when they’re ugly (I imagine, though, that children are never ugly). The second reason I won’t speak of grown-up people is that, besides being disgusting and unworthy of love, they have a compensation: they’ve eaten the apple and know good and evil, and they’ve become ‘like gods.’ They go on eating it still. But the children haven’t eaten anything, and so far they’re innocent. Are you fond of children, Alyosha? I know you are, and you’ll understand why I prefer to speak of them. If they, too, suffer horribly on earth, they must be suffering for their fathers’ sins. They must be punished for their fathers, who ate the apple. But that reasoning belongs to the other world, and the human heart here on earth can’t grasp it. The innocent must not suffer for another’s sins, and especially such innocents! You may be surprised at me, Alyosha, but I’m awfully fond of children, too. And notice that cruel people, the violent, the rapacious, the Karamazovs, are sometimes very fond of children. Children, while they’re quite little—up to seven, say—are so remote from grown-up people. They’re different creatures, almost of a different species. I knew a criminal in prison who, in the course of his career as a burglar, had murdered whole families, including several children. But when he was in prison, he had a strange affection for them. He spent all his time at his window, watching the children play in the prison yard. He trained one little boy to come up to his window and made great friends with him.... You don’t know why I’m telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches and I’m sad.”
“You speak in a strange way,” Alyosha observed uneasily, “as though you weren’t quite yourself.”

“By the way, a Bulgarian I met lately in Moscow,” Ivan went on, seeming not to hear his brother’s words, “told me about the crimes the Turks and Circassians commit all over Bulgaria, out of fear of a general rising of the Slavs. They burn villages, murder, violate women and children. They nail their prisoners by the ears to fences, leave them like that till morning, and in the morning they hang them—all sorts of things you can’t imagine. People sometimes talk of bestial cruelty, but that’s a great injustice and insult to the beasts. A beast can never be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. The tiger only tears and gnaws; that’s all he can do. He would never think of nailing people up by the ears, even if he were able to. These Turks took pleasure in torturing children, too: cutting the unborn child out of the mother’s womb, and tossing babies up in the air and catching them on the points of their bayonets before their mothers’ eyes. Doing it before the mothers’ eyes was what gave the amusement its zest. Here is another scene that I found very interesting. Imagine a trembling mother with her baby in her arms, and a circle of invading Turks around her. They’ve planned a diversion: they pet the baby and laugh to make it laugh. They succeed, and the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol four inches from the baby’s face. The baby laughs with glee and holds out its little hands to the pistol, and he pulls the trigger in the baby’s face and blows its brains out. Artistic, wasn’t it? By the way, Turks are particularly fond of sweet things, they say.”
“Brother, what are you getting at?” asked Alyosha.
“I think that if the devil doesn’t exist, and man has created him, then he has created him in his own image and likeness.”
“Just as he did God, then?” Alyosha observed.

“‘It’s wonderful how you can turn words,’ as Polonius says in _Hamlet_,” Ivan laughed. “You turn my words against me. Well, I’m glad. Yours must be a fine God, if man created Him in his image and likeness. You asked just now what I was getting at. You see, I like collecting certain facts, and, would you believe it, I even copy anecdotes of a certain sort out of newspapers and books, and I already have a fine collection. The Turks, of course, have gone into it, but they’re foreigners. I have specimens from home that are even better than the Turks. You know, we prefer beating—rods and scourges—that’s our national institution. Nailing ears is unthinkable for us, since we are, after all, Europeans. But the rod and the scourge we always have with us, and they can’t be taken from us. Abroad now they hardly do any beating. Manners are more humane, or laws have been passed, so that they don’t dare to flog men now. But they make up for it in another way, one just as national as ours. So national that it would be practically impossible among us, though I believe we’re being inoculated with it, since the religious movement began in our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, describing how, quite recently, five years ago, a murderer named Richard was executed—a young man, I believe, of twenty-three, who repented and was converted to the Christian faith at the very scaffold. This Richard was an illegitimate child, whom his parents gave away at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains. They brought him up to work for them. He grew up among them like a little wild beast. The shepherds taught him nothing, and hardly fed or clothed him. At seven they sent him out to herd the flock in cold and wet, and no one hesitated or felt any scruple about treating him so. Quite the contrary: they thought they had every right, because Richard had been given to them like a piece of property, and they didn’t even see the need to feed him. Richard himself describes how in those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash given to the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. But they wouldn’t even give him that, and beat him when he stole from the pigs. And that was how he spent all his childhood and youth, until he grew up and was strong enough to go off and be a thief. The savage began to earn his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank what he earned, lived like a brute, and ended by killing and robbing an old man. He was caught, tried, and condemned to death. They are not sentimentalists there. And in prison he was at once surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and the like. They taught him to read and write in prison, and explained the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, drummed at him incessantly, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All Geneva was in excitement about him—all philanthropic and religious Geneva. All the aristocratic and well-bred society of the town rushed to the prison, kissed Richard and embraced him: ‘You are our brother, you have found grace.’ And Richard does nothing but weep with emotion: ‘Yes, I’ve found grace! All my youth and childhood I was glad of pigs’ food, but now even I have found grace. I am dying in the Lord.’ ‘Yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you have shed blood and must die. It’s not your fault that you did not know the Lord when you coveted the pigs’ food and were beaten for stealing it (which was very wrong of you, for stealing is forbidden); but you have shed blood and you must die.’ And on the last day, Richard, completely limp, did nothing but cry and repeat every minute: ‘This is my happiest day. I am going to the Lord.’ ‘Yes,’ cry the pastors and the judges and the philanthropic ladies. ‘This is the happiest day of your life, for you are going to the Lord!’ They all walk or drive to the scaffold in procession behind the prison van. At the scaffold they call to Richard: ‘Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!’ And so, covered with his brothers’ kisses, Richard is dragged onto the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they chopped off his head in brotherly fashion, because he had found grace. Yes, that’s characteristic. That pamphlet was translated into Russian by some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank and evangelical aspirations, and has been handed out free for the enlightenment of the people. The case of Richard is interesting because it’s national. To us it’s absurd to cut off a man’s head because he has become our brother and found grace. Yet we have our own specialty, which is all but worse. Our historical pastime is the direct satisfaction of inflicting pain. There are lines in Nekrassov describing how a peasant lashes a horse across the eyes, ‘on its meek eyes’; everyone must have seen it. It’s peculiarly Russian. He describes how a feeble little nag has foundered under too heavy a load and cannot move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely, and at last beats it without knowing what he’s doing, drunk with cruelty, thrashing it mercilessly over and over. ‘However weak you are, you must pull, if you die for it.’ The nag strains, and then he begins lashing the poor defenseless creature across its weeping, its ‘meek eyes.’ The frantic beast tugs and drags the load, trembling all over, gasping for breath, moving sideways, with a sort of unnatural, spasmodic action—it’s awful in Nekrassov. But that’s only a horse, and God gave us horses to be beaten. So the Tatars taught us, and they left us the knout as a reminder. But men can be beaten, too. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife beat their own child with a birch-rod, a girl of seven. I have an exact account of it. The papa was glad that the birch was covered with twigs. ‘It stings more,’ said he, and so he began stinging his daughter. I know for a fact that there are people who are worked up to sensuality at every blow, literal sensuality, which grows steadily with every blow they deal. They beat for a minute, for five minutes, for ten minutes, more often and more savagely. The child screams. At last the child cannot scream; it gasps, ‘Daddy! daddy!’ By some diabolical, unseemly chance the case was brought into court. A lawyer is hired. The Russian people have long called a barrister ‘a conscience for hire.’ The lawyer protests in his client’s defense. ‘It’s such a simple thing,’ he says, ‘an everyday domestic event. A father corrects his child. To our shame, it is brought into court.’ The jury, convinced by him, gives a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer is acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn’t there! I would have proposed raising a subscription in his honor! Charming pictures.”

“But I have still better things about children. I’ve collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five who was hated by her father and mother, ‘most worthy and respectable people, of good education and breeding.’ You see, I have to repeat it again: it’s a peculiar characteristic of many people, this love of torturing children, and children only. To every other type of humanity these torturers behave mildly and benevolently, like cultivated and humane Europeans. But they are very fond of tormenting children, even fond of children themselves in that sense. It’s just their defenselessness that tempts the tormentor, just the angelic trust of the child, who has no refuge and no appeal, that sets his vile blood on fire. In every man, of course, a demon lies hidden—the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of the tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off the chain, the demon of the diseases that follow on vice, gout, kidney disease, and so on.
